title: The Challenge isn’t Prediction—it’s Positioning - Systematic Investor - Ep.359

meta.source: Macro Transcripts/The Challenge isn’t Prediction—it’s Positioning - Systematic Investor - Ep.359.docx

speakers: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher; surname garbled in captions)
summary: Systematic Investor 359: why positioning and timing matter more than prediction. Equities extrapolate while bonds mean revert, trend profits in bonds track central banks, liquidity is fragile and costly for trend followers, bubbles are friendly to trend following, and model complexity vs causal simplicity.

coverage.note: intro; China trip observations on digital economy
digital payments outage; golf/Parkinson aside; Fed dissent
Fed history; copper tariff drop; timing; trend update starts
CTA index numbers; equities extrapolative vs bonds mean reverting
fixed income fair value; trend by sector
central bank dominance; macro trends; sudden stops
stablecoin interest; tokenized MMFs; bubbles intro
bubble behavior, fire analogy, Gerro exit rule
trend followers and bubbles; cocoa; regulators
nothing actionable: sign-off and sponsor read

completeness_estimate: 0.80 - the first reader caught almost every main theme (extrapolative vs mean-reverting markets, central-bank trend, liquidity costs, bubbles, complexity vs causality); missing items are mostly supporting data (YTD index returns, Fed history) and a few side topics.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: two descendants, uh Waller Bowman, um were in favor of a rate cut.
claims.claim: At the July 2025 FOMC two dissenters (Waller, Bowman), both candidates to replace Powell, favored a cut while the chair showed no hurry, pointing to political pressure on the Fed.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: there was a historic drop in the price of copper yesterday. The US uh copper I should say of about 20%.
claims.claim: US copper fell about 20% in a day after a change in the Trump tariff policy, hurting trend followers who held long copper after a breakout.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: timing is everything is that we may have a pretty good idea of what may happen. We just don't know
claims.claim: We often know what should happen (inflation, slowdown) but not when, so timing rather than the why determines returns.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: if they believe that inflation is going to be going lower and so they say well we don't need to
claims.claim: The Fed faces a dilemma between a slowing economy (inflation lower) and robust growth (inflation higher), so it takes a precautionary stance because tariff pass-through is unknown.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: my own trend barometer actually finished yesterday at 55.
claims.claim: July 2025 trend-follower performance was modestly positive: oil complex up about 10%, equities up, dollar index up 3% (best week since 2022), grains in downtrend, copper reversal; Beta 50 +0.67% July.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: equity markets are extrapolative. So that usually they're going to continue on in a longer term trend.
claims.claim: Equity markets are extrapolative (trending, with investor optimism) while fixed income markets are mean reverting and range-bound as they move to fair value.
claims.direction: trend in equities; fade extremes in bonds
claims.conditions: fixed income mean reverts around fair value
claims.testable: yes - test autocorrelation by asset class

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the fair valuation is always what is expected inflation
claims.claim: Fair value of a 10-year is expected inflation (about 2.5%) plus expected growth (2-2.5%), giving a 4.5-5% yield, which anchors the range in bonds.
claims.indicator: 10-year yield vs expected inflation plus growth
claims.testable: yes - regress yields on inflation and growth expectations

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Even though we think of equities as being something that always goes up to the uh top right corner, actually from a trend following perspective, they're not that great.
claims.claim: Over the last 20 years trend followers have made more money in bonds than in equities, despite bonds being thought of as mean-reverting, because trending in bonds follows the Fed.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: what you're really picking up in fixed income on quote unquote trend is uh the long policy movements of a central bank.
claims.claim: Trend profits in fixed income reflect long central bank policy cycles, which suit trend following, whereas equity trends are harder because of sudden short-term volatility.
claims.testable: partly - link trend to policy moves

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: macro trends lead to price trends. So, uh price trends are a description of what's happening in the underlying economy.
claims.claim: Price trends in bonds follow trends in underlying inflation, which are gradual and persistent, so trend following captures macro trends; macro direction is easy to attribute ex post but hard to predict.
claims.direction: trend in bond prices follows inflation

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: we're facing more sudden stops in the economy
claims.claim: Sudden stops (events causing large moves that reverse quickly) have replaced longer high-volatility spells, which hurts trend followers.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the number of factors that are necessary or needed to explain what is going on in the economy and markets is much greater than maybe what we've saw in years past.
claims.claim: Markets are more complex now: more factors are needed than the simple growth/inflation/term premium model for bonds or earnings/rates for equities.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the when is the more important
claims.claim: Economists agree on what tariffs will do (hurt prices, earnings) but not when, so timing matters more than the reason for making money.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: good portfolio construction is based on do on a do nothing principle and a do nothing principle will say you know find your weights and leave it alone.
claims.claim: Do-nothing: a fixed allocation beat trying to react to tariffs; a 'do nothing plus' strategy adds trend-following, holding rising assets and reducing falling ones.
claims.direction: hold rising assets; cut falling assets
claims.testable: yes - compare static and trend-overlay portfolios

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the current environment is uh is leading to politicians to be less muted in their uh in their statements and that causes the the market to react quicker which causes this these sudden shocks.
claims.claim: Less muted political statements cause fast shocks; systematic traders must react, are pulled away from do-nothing, and get whipsawed when statements reverse.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: markets seem to be less liquid today than what they may have been in the past.
claims.claim: Liquidity is more fragile (bid-ask spreads narrower but depth more volatile with fat tails) due to central bank activity, larger sovereign debt supply and undercapitalised dealers, so liquidity disappears in stress.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: generally trend followers are liquidity takers not liquidity providers.
claims.claim: Trend followers pay for liquidity, so illiquidity and crowding raise transaction costs that can be a significant share of return in weak years; controlling costs is the real battle.
claims.conditions: more trend followers on the same side

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: right now there are about $280 billion in stable coin.
claims.claim: The claim that stablecoins create new demand for Treasury bills is weak because stablecoin money may merely come out of bank reserves already held in T-bills.
claims.testable: partly - net new T-bill holdings unknown

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: you don't get that interest. It's the stable coin issuer that's actually making that interest.
claims.claim: Holders of stablecoins forgo interest, which accrues to the issuer; tokenized money market funds (JPMorgan, BNY) that keep interest while serving as collateral are more important for credit market health.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: What we find is is that when you look at you know extreme price movements that usually that they last longer than what we expect.
claims.claim: Research on bubbles shows that extreme price moves last longer than expected and often do not fully reverse; the worst case is when everyone calls it a bubble yet keeps buying.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the market structure is your oxygen u you know your heat is speculation and then the fuel is leverage
claims.claim: Bubble fire analogy: market structure (liquidity) is oxygen, speculation is heat, leverage is fuel; leverage is harder to get now, so the fuel is limited.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: you look at past price extremes be able to look at the statistical behavior of the prices and say if it you goes a little sort of parabolic or it goes more exponential.
claims.claim: Cornell professor Gerro proposes exiting a bubble when prices go parabolic or exponential relative to past extremes; Mark doubts it identifies the top.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: from a trend followers perspective you want to embrace or love the bubble.
claims.claim: Trend followers profit from bubbles (cocoa, orange juice, gold) by riding the trend and exiting by signal or stop-loss; speculative longs in cocoa actually fell before the peak, contradicting regulator claims.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: you want to make models as complex as possible meaning use as many factors as you can
claims.claim: Kelly (AQR/Yale) argues for complex machine-learning models with many factors since prediction, not explanation, matters; traditionalists warn complexity leads to overfitting; simple models reach about 90% of the prediction.

correction.issue: Blends three sources: Kelly argues for complex ML models with many factors, traditionalists warn of overfitting, but the 'simple models reach about 90% of the prediction' result comes from a separate fixed-income/equity-correlation paper (135 factors), not from Kelly.
correction.fix: Kelly (AQR/Yale) argues for complex machine-learning models with many factors since prediction, not explanation, matters; traditionalists warn that complexity leads to overfitting and that limited factors do better over the long run.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: causal inference has said like let's make sure that we only add factors that we know that we think cause you know an impact on stocks
claims.claim: Causal inference requires only factors with a measurable causal impact, shifting the debate from simple vs complex to causal vs spurious.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the coefficients or the models that you use
claims.claim: Model coefficients (e.g. housing models) are unstable over time, so more complexity increases instability and overfitting risk; wisdom lies in simplification.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: We're just going to go with the flow.
claims.claim: Trend following is designed for an unknown future (energy, AI, dark factories could change the world), since it adapts along the way rather than predicting.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: prices are primal and that that whatever the future that starts to evolve will be revealed in prices.
claims.claim: Because nobody can predict energy costs, leaders or the Fed, one should follow prices which reveal the future as quickly as possible.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: it really has, uh, turned into a digital economy, at least for the major cities
claims.claim: After a China trip, Mark reports a cashless digital economy in major cities (Alipay, WeChat), advanced EVs and visible innovation: structural evidence of China's technological momentum.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Denmark had an outage of the main electronic payment system, uh, only a couple of weeks ago
claims.claim: A cashless economy has a single-point-of-failure weakness: a payment-system outage in Denmark (and Spain) stopped card payments, so digital convenience trades against resilience.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: in 1990 uh with Alan Greenspan uh who told Congress that he would lower interest rate but only if they cut the deficit
claims.claim: Historically Fed chairs set fiscal conditions for cuts (Greenspan 1990, Volcker 1985 asked for about a $50B deficit cut), unlike today when the president pressures the Fed.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: I think the issue of Fed independence is something that's just overhanging a lot of thinking, especially in the fixed income markets.
claims.claim: Doubt about Fed independence weighs on fixed-income markets and adds to the difficulty of knowing the Fed's reaction function.
claims.testable: partly - term premium and curve shape proxy it

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the Btop 50 was up 67 basis points in July and it's down only 2.6% for the month of uh sorry for the year.
claims.claim: Trend followers were still negative year to date at end-July 2025 (BTOP50 -2.6%, SG CTA Index -6.82%, SG Trend -8.88%, Short Term Traders -4.76%) versus MSCI World +10.5% and S&P 500 +9%, so CTAs lagged equities after the April reversal.
claims.indicator: BTOP50, SG CTA Index, SG Trend, SG Short Term Traders, MSCI World, S&P 500
claims.direction: trend lags equities after V-shaped reversal

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: we know that yield curves have to be slightly upward sloping in general. the inversion of uh yield curves for years.
claims.claim: A slightly upward-sloping yield curve is the normal state and the years of inversion under QE were an anomaly, which is why fixed income mean-reverts toward fair value.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: we'll probably say that the dominant player in fixed income is still central banks. even more so than what it was in the past.
claims.claim: Identify the dominant player per market: central banks dominate fixed income (even more than before), so trend in bonds is a trend in central-bank behaviour and the strategy is exposed to a change of central-bank view.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: bonds have been better to trade for trend followers but haven't been better for the last two years that's for sure.
claims.claim: Bonds were the better trend sector over the long run, but for the last two years bond (and equity) trend profits have been poor because of V-shaped corrections and constant flipping of fixed-income exposure.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: Maybe you could say it's consensus without real conviction.
claims.claim: In 2025 recession risk is seen as low and inflation as subdued, yet nobody trusts the calm: consensus without conviction.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: the stable coin may have a uh a usage case for when there's high transactions.
claims.claim: Stablecoins have real use cases only where transaction fees are high (emerging markets) or to replace black-market cash; US payments are cheap, so net new Treasury demand is small.
claims.testable: partly - stablecoin supply and reserves are public

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: the 85ish% that the NASDAQ dropped since then
claims.claim: Bubbles used to be feared because of the aftermath (Nasdaq fell about 85% after 2000), but they now seem normal, so the label 'bubble' matters less for decisions.

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: How did we go within a short period of 6 months from a a doomsday scenario to uh to a bubble scenario?
claims.claim: Narrative can flip from doomsday (tariffs and slow growth) to bubble within six months, so the story is a poor basis for positioning; the prices are what matter.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: many investors won't be able or allowed to invest in funds that trades commodities because they think inherently that we um are part of the reason why commodity prices from time to time goes higher
claims.claim: Regulators and some European investors treat trend followers as a cause of commodity price rises, so commodity-trading CTAs face institutional restrictions (reputational, not statistical, risk).

claims.speaker: Mark (guest, systematic macro researcher)
claims.quote: simple models actually do really well will get you saying 90% of the way so the added factors you know they they contribute but they don't you know add substant atively to your your overall prediction.
claims.claim: A study of fixed-income/equity correlation with about 135 factors finds simple models get about 90% of the prediction; extra factors add little unless machine-learning methods are used, in which case more factors help.
claims.conditions: Extra factors help only with ML techniques.

claims.speaker: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
claims.quote: complexity can be somewhat uh seductive meaning that we may mistake model sophistication, if we call it that, for better market understanding.
claims.claim: Complexity is seductive: sophisticated models can be mistaken for better market understanding, and the failure shows only when it is too late.
